title: My GrandOrgue Implementation
text:
Executive Summary
This site documents my experience setting up, configuring, and using a GrandOrgue virtual pipe organ (VPO). As of 2026, there was little compiled documentation other than how to download. Information such as system and hardware requirements was scattered throughout the internet, but one generally had to find it through a search engine. The official software documentation consisted of various help pages, but no step-by-step instructions. Lots of community user experiences were captured in hundreds of issues and thousands of discussions on the official GitHub repo. Most of the information here came from those sources.
Getting a functioning VPO took considerable trial and error. The dead ends and failures are not contained here, but important “gotchas” are noted when helpful.
These pages are my contribution to the open source GrandOrgue project and its outstanding user community. I hope these pages help you build your own GrandOrgue VPO.

title: 1  Hardware
text:
1.2 Discussion
GrandOrgue is free open source computer software supported for Windows, MacOS, and at least some Linux distributions. System and hardware requirements are summarized here, with the most important requirement being RAM.
My initial installation was intended to proof-of-concept learning experiment to assess whether or not it was something I wanted to delve further into and scale up. I already had an old (circa 1997) Casio MIDI keyboard1, so I decided to use that as the workbench test case for experimentation. Then, once I knew what I was doing and felt comfortable with the technical components, I wanted to transfer the setup to a MIDI-ready digital church organ to try it out “in the field” with an actual organ console, decent speakers, and a room where an organ is regularly used.
With this in mind, I sought portability with minimal spatial footprint. Desktop computers took up too much space and are not easily portable, so they were out. Without having a personal organ at home, I needed to interface with the software directly through the computer rather than via an organ console, so I wanted to have a touch screen monitor that could be positioned in close proximity to the music keyboard. While standard laptops with touch screens are portable and could work, I would have to always reach over the laptop keyboard to reach the screen, which was not ideal. My solution was to use a Raspberry Pi together with a simple touch screen monitor.
I opted for the Raspberry Pi 5 because it was the first and, as of 2026, only unit to support 16 GB of RAM. I purchased a full starter kit for $385 which included:

Raspberry Pi 5 with 2.4Ghz 64-bit quad-core CPU and 64 GB of RAM
128GB Micro SD Card pre-loaded with 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, USB MicroSD Card Reader
Plastic protective case
Low noise bearing system fan
Heat sink
45W PD Power Supply
2 6-foot display cables

I bought a simple and compact 15.6” portable touch screen monitor for $95 as my primary means of interacting with GrandOrgue. An upgrade might be in store down the road, but this will due to start.
Unfortunately, the Raspberry Pi 5 does not have a dedicated 3.5mm headphone audio jack like its predecessor. Audio is outputted through HDMI or USB instead. I ended up buying a Behringer UMC204HD USB audio interface for $116 which would allow me to use a single USB port for both audio and to connect standard MIDI cables instead of a MIDI-USB cable. I also bought a 9.8-foot dual 5-pin MIDI cable for $11 to go along with that because I did not have one already.
Altogether, my expenses for the initial set up came out to be just over $600:

title: 2  Set-up
text:
2.1 Raspberry Pi setup
Raspberry Pi (RPi) devices run Debian-based Raspberry Pi OS. GrandOrgue needs the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS in order to utilize all of the installed RAM (a 32-bit OS would cap the usable RAM at 4 GB, regardless of what is installed in the system.) This comes pre-installed on the CanaKit RPi.
If you don’t have the 64-bit version:
Back on the RPi, before installing anything, download and install any OS updates:
GrandOrgue recommends X11 to properly handle window sizing and positioning. To switch the display mode:
The touch monitor is plug-and-play. Since the RPi 5 only has a single USB-C port, which is used for the power supply, the monitor needs to be connected to the RPi via both HDMI for data and USB for power. I used the HDMI to mini-HDMI cable that came with the RPi and the USB-C to USB-A cable that came with the monitor. The RPi did need to be rebooted after everything was plugged in for the touch screen to work properly.

title: 2  Set-up
text:
2.2 GrandOrgue installation
From the GrandOrgue releases GitHub, download the arm64.deb architecture package. As of May 2026, the current release was grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb. You can also download it directly in the terminal:
wget https://github.com/GrandOrgue/grandorgue/releases/download/3.17.1-1/grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb

(Note: grandorgue requires wxWidgets 3.2 and grandorgue-wx30 requires wxWidgets 3.0. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships with wxWidgets 3.2, so the standard grandorgue package above is the correct one.)
Install the software using either the downloaded installer or terminal:
sudo apt install ./grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb
You might get a Permission Denied warning, but it can be ignored:
N: Download is performed unsandboxed as root as file '/home/username/grandorgue_3.17.1-1_arm64.deb' couldn't be accessed by user '_apt'. - pkgAcquire::Run (13: Permission denied)
It is not a fatal error; the application should have installed fine.
Verify the installation by looking for it in the Sound & Video application menu. Launch the program. It should open with the demo organ available.

2.2.1 MIDI
Next, configure the MIDI hardware:

Plug in the Behringer UMC204HD USB audio interface to the RPi via USB and to the keyboard or organ using MIDI cables.
Open GrandOrgue and go to File → Preferences → Audio. You should see the UMC204HD listed as an ALSA device. Select it, set the sample rate to 48000 Hz and start with 512 samples per buffer.
You can tune the buffer size down later if latency feels sluggish, or up if you hear crackle.
Go to File → Preferences → MIDI Devices. The UMC204HD’s MIDI ports should appear as ALSA MIDI devices.
Enable the input port. Then load a sample set and use File → MIDI Recorder or just play a key. GrandOrgue will prompt you to map MIDI channels to manuals the first time.



2.2.2 GrandOrgue configuration
Lastly, we need to map MIDI channels between GrandOrgue and the instrument.

Go to File → Settings → MIDI Devices
Under “MIDI output devices”, make sure UNC204HD is selected. Click OK.
On the virtual pipe organ (VPO) console, right-click a virtual manual to map to.
In the box that opens, click “Listen for Event”. Play a key on the keyboard you wish to map to that virtual organ manual.
Click OK.

To reduce audio lag:

File → Settings → Audio
Set the “Samples per buffer” to 256 or 128 (defaults to 512).

The lower the buffer size, the lower the latency. At 48,000 Hz sample rate, 128 samples per buffer supposedly gives about 2.7 milliseconds of latency, which is completely imperceptible. The tradeoff is that very low buffer sizes can cause audio crackle or dropouts if the RPi can’t process audio fast enough, but the Pi 5 should be plenty powerful enough to handle 128 samples without trouble, especially with the demo sample set.
Even at 128, I still noticed a lag, but it was better than when I started. It is possible that some delay is “built in” as the result of the sample recording. This remains to be determined. I am accustomed to old-technology, non-realistic digital organs where the sound is instantaneous, where many pipe organs have a slight (fraction of a second) lag between the time a key is depressed and the sound is actually heard.


2.2.3 Audio
By default, the VPO plays through the computer speakers. In this setup, this means the speakers on the touch screen monitor. Much better sound quality can be obtained with better speakers or headphones.
Bluetooth headphones may experience a fairly significant lag in audio. It did for me. Since my old keyboard did not have an Audio In jack, I could not channel the sound back to the keyboard speakers – which is just as well, because they are not very good either. The best (but not perfect) option was wired headphones plugged into the UNC204HD interface. The only headphones I owned had a 1/8” plug, so I had to use a 1/4”-1/8” adapter to connect them. There was a slight buzz, possibly resulting from the extra connection. It was annoying, but not bad enough to abandon the setup.

title: 4  Customization
text:
4.1 Bureå Funeral Chapel
The default sample set is great to get started with, but it’s rather small. The beauty of virtual pipe organ (VPO) software is the ability and flexibility to use any number of sample sets. Many sample sets of various sizes exist, from small single-division organs to large many-division instruments. One constraint is disk storage: one needs to have enough space to download and store the sample set. The primary constraint with choosing samples to use, however, is one’s memory: the sample set must fit in the computer’s RAM to work properly. Thus, my constraint was 16 GB RAM that came on the Raspberry Pi 5. What this means in practice:
Since I only had one keyboard with no pedalboard, it made sense to consider single-manual samples. I could use larger ones, but I could only play one manual. The workaround would be mapping the Great division to my keyboard and relying on couplers to play other manuals from the Great manual.
The first organ I tried was the Bureå Funeral Chapel from Lars Virtual Pipe Organs. This is a small chamber organ with one manual, pedals, and 9 stops. All of the manual stops are split stops with separate drawknobs for bass (first two octaves) and division. This provides greater flexibility on a small instrument, allowing the organist to use different combinations of stops on one manual instead of across two manuals.
First, I downloaded the .rar file. I needed to install the “unrar” utility the first time in order to extract this:
Then I unpacked it into the GrandOrgue/Organs/ directory:
Open GrandOrgue, then got to File → Open, find and select the desired organ sample, and click “Open”. If everything worked, the new organ should load and be ready for use.

sudo apt install unrar

unrar x Burea_Funeral_Chapel.rar /home/username/GrandOrgue/Organs/Burea_Funeral_Chapel/

title: 5  Rendering
text:
5.1 Step 1. Make sure you have a recent RStudio
The repo includes a GitHub Action that will render (build) the website automatically when you make changes to the files. It will be pushed to the gh-pages branch.
But when you are developing your content, you will want to render it locally.
Have you updated RStudio since about August 2022? No? Then update to a newer version of RStudio. In general, you want to keep RStudio updated and it is required to have a recent version to use Quarto.

title: 5  Rendering
section: 5.2 Step 2. Clone and create RStudio project
text:
5.2 Step 2. Clone and create RStudio project
First, clone the repo onto your local computer. How? You can click File > New Project and then select “Version Control”. Paste in the url of the repository. That will clone the repo on to your local computer. When you make changes, you will need to push those up.

title: 5  Rendering
text:
5.3 Step 3. Render within RStudio
RStudio will recognize that this is a Quarto project by the presence of the _quarto.yml file and will see the “Build” tab. Click the “Render website” button to render to the _site folder.
Previewing: You can either click index.html in the _site folder and specify “preview in browser” or set up RStudio to preview to the viewer panel. To do the latter, go to Tools > Global Options > R Markdown. Then select “Show output preview in: Viewer panel”.

title: 6  References
text:
Quarto has powerful references functionality. You can easily insert citations from Zotero libraries that you maintain in the cloud (on Zotero). This allows the whole team to update the library and you can sync up to that library. Read about this on the Quarto documentation on citations. Google youtube videos on this also to see it in action.
Add a .bib file in to your project or add a linked Zotero library via RStudio in Visual mode with Tools > Project Options… > R Markdown > select custom libraries from the Zotero dropdown.
The you can type @ and you will see a dropdown of the references in your libraries. You can then select the ones to add. If you don’t see the one you need, you can paste in the DOI and it will be added to your references file (with all the info). The references will be added to your references section of your book automatically.
See the references.qmd file for how to include the references.

@ansley1981 will produce Ansley and Davis (1981)
[@ansley1981] will produce (Ansley and Davis 1981).





Ansley, H. L. H., and C. D. Davis. 1981. Migration and Standing Stock of Fishes Associated with Artificial and Natural Reefs on Georgia’s Outer Continental Shelf. Brunswick, Georgia, USA.
